stem: What is the lower fixed point of the Celsius scale?

options.content: The temperature of pure melting ice, 0 °C
The temperature of the human body
The steam point of pure boiling water, 100 °C
options.rationale: That is the upper fixed point.

options.content: Absolute zero
options.rationale: Not used as a fixed point here.

explanation: The ice point, pure melting ice, defines 0 °C.

stem: Which change makes a liquid-in-glass thermometer more sensitive?

options.content: A smaller bulb
options.rationale: A larger bulb is more sensitive.

options.content: A thicker glass wall
A shorter tube
A narrower bore (tube)
options.rationale: Correct: the same expansion gives a longer movement.

explanation: A narrower bore (and a larger bulb) makes the liquid move further for each degree.

stem: An uncalibrated thermometer has a liquid column $3.0\ \text{cm}$ long at the ice point and $28.0\ \text{cm}$ long at the steam point. What temperature does a column of $13.0\ \text{cm}$ show?
explanation: $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is $25.0\ \text{cm}$, so $1\ \text{cm} = 4\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Rise above the ice point $= 13.0 - 3.0 = 10.0\ \text{cm}$, so $\theta = 40\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
workedSolution: 1. $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is $25.0\ \text{cm}$, so $1\ \text{cm} = 4\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Rise above the ice point $= 13.0 - 3.0 = 10.0\ \text{cm}$, so $\theta = 40\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
hints: Find how many °C each cm represents.
Measure from the ice-point length, not from zero.

stem: Why does a clinical thermometer have a constriction (narrow kink) just above the bulb?

options.content: To make it more sensitive to small changes in the patient's temperature
options.rationale: Sensitivity comes from the narrow bore.

options.content: To stop the liquid expanding past the top of the scale
So the liquid thread stays put after it is taken from the patient
To make the range of temperatures it can measure wider

explanation: The constriction breaks the thread when the liquid contracts, so the highest reading can be read later.

stem: Which thermometer is best for measuring the temperature inside a furnace at about 1000 °C?

options.content: A mercury-in-glass thermometer
options.rationale: Mercury boils at 357 °C and glass would soften.

options.content: A thermocouple
An alcohol thermometer
A clinical thermometer

explanation: Thermocouples have a very wide range and can withstand high temperatures.
hints: Compare the range of each thermometer.

stem: Why is alcohol, not mercury, used in thermometers for very cold places?

options.content: Alcohol is easier to see in the cold because it is dyed.
options.rationale: It is dyed, but that is not the reason.

options.content: Alcohol freezes at a much lower temperature than mercury.
Alcohol boils at a higher temperature than mercury does.
Mercury expands too much in very cold weather.

explanation: Mercury freezes at −39 °C; alcohol stays liquid down to about −115 °C.

stem: Match each thermometer with its thermometric property.

right.content: Voltage produced at a junction of two metals

explanation: Each thermometer uses a property that changes steadily with temperature.

stem: What name is given to a physical property that changes with temperature and can be used to measure it?
explanation: It is a thermometric property, for example the length of a liquid column.

stem: A thermocouple responds quickly to temperature changes because its junction is very small.
explanation: The tiny junction has very little mass to heat or cool, so it reaches the surrounding temperature quickly.

stem: A learner is asked to mark a scale on an unmarked mercury-in-glass thermometer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how she marks the two fixed points.

points.description: Places the bulb in pure melting ice and marks the mercury level as 0 °C (ice point)
Places the bulb in steam above pure boiling water at standard pressure and marks the level as 100 °C (steam point)

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How does she complete the scale?

points.description: Divides the distance between the two marks into 100 equal divisions (degrees)

explanation: Mark the ice and steam points, then divide the gap into 100 equal degrees.
hints: What two reproducible temperatures are used?
